drafts.dataLed:
Park Lane is now the sixth cheapest street on the board.

On the 1935 board it was second dearest. That is the whole post, really.

I rebuilt the classic London board with 2026 prices — every figure pulled from HM Land Registry open data, Price Paid Data and the UK House Price Index, under the Open Government Licence v3.0. No subscription data anywhere.

The ladder has been turned upside down.

Bond Street was 20th of 22 on the printed board. It is now 1st, at £33,575,353 — and that figure needs its caveat said in the same breath: it is a median price paid, and on a handful of streets the method mixes some commercial transfers in. That is disclosed on the square itself.

Regent Street moved furthest: 18th to 4th cheapest.
Bow Street went from mid-board to 2nd cheapest.
Old Kent Road hasn't moved. £60 then, £325,000 now, still last. The one rung the old board still gets right.

The 1935 ladder spanned 6.7x top to bottom. The recorded 2026 evidence spans 103x.

But the prices aren't the point.

The point is a rule: no number reaches the screen without a traceable source.

There is a check that runs on every load. It sweeps 141 monetary values, roughly 1,700 text nodes and 99 strings baked into the 3D textures, and it asks one question of each — where did you come from. If a single value can't answer, the game does not start. It prints the reason and stops. It is an absence check, not a spot check.

I didn't want to take my own word for it, so I attacked it. Eight adversarial injections: an unsourced value tagged as though it were traced, an untagged value, a banned term, a fabricated figure baked into a WebGL texture, an undeclared numeral, two invented round numbers whose entire rounding band contains no real transaction. All eight caught.

21 of the 22 streets carry an actual HM Land Registry transaction ID and URI. Trafalgar Square has no residential sale on record at all, so it falls back to the borough HPI average — and the square says so, on its face.

The same discipline applied to the event cards. 21 survived, sourced to gov.uk, the Bank of England and the ONS. 14 were rejected as unverifiable — including "commercial EPC C by 2027, B by 2030", which half our industry repeats as settled law. The 2027 and 2030 commercial EPC targets remain consultation, not enacted law. A second fact-check then corrected 7 more cards whose wording overstated its own source.

Why a board game? Because it is the worst possible venue, deliberately chosen.

A board game is the one format where invented prices are traditional. Nobody has ever asked where the £200 came from. If the rule holds up somewhere that frivolous, it holds up in a lender covenant pack.

What it isn't: the data panel still hasn't passed its own Financial Times standards review — 71 out of 82 at the last check. Bond Street at £33.6m (rounded) is effectively unbuyable on the opening capital. The median method has the commercial-transfer issue above.

It's an original homage to Elizabeth Magie's The Landlord's Game, 1904, US Patent 748,626, public domain. You win on rent roll, not on the size of your pile.

It is live at [URL]. Find a number on that board that has no source behind it. If you find one, tell me and I will publish the fix and credit you.

Sources, licence attribution, method notes and the full list of rejected claims in the first comment.

If you would rather see this rule applied to a lender covenant pack or a valuation model than to a board game, message me.
drafts.storyLed:
In 1904 a woman patented a board game to prove that land monopoly was harmful.

The commercial version that followed kept her board and inverted her argument.

Elizabeth Magie, The Landlord's Game, US Patent 748,626, now public domain. In her design you won on rent roll — income, not pile size. I've kept that scoring rule, because it is the only honest one, and because it made the rest of what I wanted to test possible.

I rebuilt her board with the classic London streets and real 2026 prices.

Every price fetched from HM Land Registry open data — Price Paid Data and the UK House Price Index, Open Government Licence v3.0. No subscription sources.

Then the board did something I didn't design.

Park Lane, second dearest in 1935, is now the sixth cheapest street on it. Bond Street was 20th of 22 on the printed board and is now 1st, at £33,575,353 — a median price paid, and on a few streets that method pulls in some commercial transfers, which is disclosed on the square. Regent Street moved 18th to 4th cheapest. Bow Street, mid-board then, second cheapest now. Old Kent Road hasn't budged: £60 then, £325,000 now, still last.

The old ladder spanned 6.7x from top to bottom. The evidence spans 103x.

Four of the 22 squares still sit exactly where 1935 put them. The other eighteen tell you what eighty years of London did to the ranking property people carry around in their heads.

That is the fun part. Here is the actual experiment.

I wanted to know whether a rule I use in client work survives contact with the least serious thing I could build. The rule is simple: no number reaches the screen without a traceable source.

So the build carries a gate. On every load it sweeps 141 monetary values, roughly 1,700 text nodes and 99 strings baked into the 3D textures, and asks each one where it came from. If any single value cannot answer, the game refuses to start and prints the reason. Absence check, not spot check.

Then I attacked it, because an untested gate is a decoration. Eight adversarial injections — an unsourced number tagged as if traced, an untagged number, a banned term, a fabricated figure baked into a texture, an undeclared numeral, two invented round numbers whose whole rounding band contains no real transaction. All eight caught.

21 of the 22 streets carry a real HM Land Registry transaction ID and URI. Trafalgar Square has no residential sale on record at all, so it falls back to the borough HPI average, and the square says so.

The event cards got the same treatment. 21 kept, sourced to gov.uk, the Bank of England and the ONS. 14 rejected as unverifiable — including "commercial EPC C by 2027, B by 2030", which is repeated across our industry as settled law. The 2027 and 2030 commercial EPC targets remain consultation, not enacted law. A second fact-check then corrected 7 more cards that overstated their own sources.

A board game is the worst possible venue for that rule, which is exactly why I chose it. Invented prices are traditional here. Nobody has ever asked where the £200 came from. If the discipline holds in a place this frivolous, it holds in a lender pack.

Honest about where it falls short: the data panel has not passed its own Financial Times standards review — 71 out of 82 at the last check. The median price paid method mixes some commercial transfers into a few streets. And Bond Street at £33.6m (rounded) is effectively unbuyable on the opening capital, which is either a design flaw or the most accurate thing on the board.

It is live at [URL]. Find a number on that board that has no source behind it. If you find one, tell me and I will publish the fix and credit you.

Sources, licence attribution, method notes and the full list of rejected claims are in the first comment.

If you would rather see this rule applied to a lender covenant pack or a valuation model than to a board game, message me.
drafts.craftLed:
I built something that refuses to start if it finds an unsourced number.

Not a warning. It stops, and it prints which number and why.

That is the actual product of the last day's work. The thing it happens to be attached to is a playable 3D board game of classic London streets, priced at 2026, which I will come to.

The rule first, because the rule is the point.

No monetary value reaches the screen without a chain back to a single facts file. A check runs on every load and sweeps 141 money values, roughly 1,700 text nodes and 99 strings baked into the 3D textures. Each one has to say where it came from. One failure and nothing renders.

It is an absence check, not a spot check. It does not sample. It asks the whole surface.

Then I attacked it, because a gate you haven't tried to break is decoration. Eight adversarial injections:

An unsourced value tagged as though it had been traced. An untagged value. A banned term. Trade dress. A fabricated figure baked into a WebGL texture where no text search would reach it. An undeclared numeral. Two invented rounded values whose entire rounding band contains no real transaction.

All eight caught.

Now the venue, and the choice was deliberate.

A board game is the worst possible place to enforce this. It is the one format where invented prices are traditional — nobody in a hundred years has asked where the £200 came from. That is precisely why I put the rule there. If it survives somewhere this frivolous, it survives in a lender covenant pack.

So every price on the board is real. HM Land Registry open data, Price Paid Data and the UK House Price Index, Open Government Licence v3.0. No subscription data anywhere. 21 of the 22 streets carry an actual transaction ID and URI. Trafalgar Square has no residential sale on record at all, so it falls back to the borough HPI average, and the square says so on its face.

And the real data does something a made-up board never could.

Park Lane, second dearest in 1935, is now the sixth cheapest square. Bond Street was 20th of 22 and is now 1st, at £33,575,353 — a median price paid, and on a handful of streets that method mixes in some commercial transfers, which is disclosed on the square. Regent Street moved 18th to 4th cheapest. Old Kent Road hasn't moved at all: £60 then, £325,000 now, still last.

The printed ladder spanned 6.7x. The recorded evidence spans 103x.

The same discipline ran over the event cards. 21 kept, each sourced to gov.uk, the Bank of England or the ONS. 14 rejected as unverifiable — among them "commercial EPC C by 2027, B by 2030", which a great deal of UK CRE repeats as law. The 2027 and 2030 commercial EPC targets remain consultation, not enacted law. A second adversarial fact-check then corrected 7 more cards whose wording overstated its own source.

On whether it looks like a toy — that gets tested too, not asserted. Screenshots were compared against real screenshots of Catan Universe with labels stripped, at matched dimensions, three independent judges per comparison, positions swapped, run twice. Desktop 2-1 to ours both runs. Mobile 3-0 both runs. Draw your own conclusion from that; it is a method, not a scalp.

Where it falls short, in my own words rather than yours: the data panel has not passed its own Financial Times standards review — 71 out of 82 at the last check. The median price paid method has the commercial-transfer problem noted above. Bond Street at £33.6m (rounded) is effectively unbuyable on the opening capital.

Provenance: an original homage to Elizabeth Magie's The Landlord's Game, 1904, US Patent 748,626, public domain. You win on rent roll, not on the size of your pile — which was her point.

It is live at [URL]. Find a number on that board that has no source behind it. If you find one, tell me and I will publish the fix and credit you.

Sources, licence attribution, method notes and the list of rejected claims are in the first comment.

If you would rather see this rule applied to a lender covenant pack or a valuation model than to a board game, message me.
drafts.videoScript:
LANDLORD: LONDON 2026 — 24 seconds, square 1:1, captions burned in, no voiceover, no music with vocals, no logo sting. Must read fully with sound off. All on-screen text in the same single sans face, high contrast, safe-margin 8% from every edge.

0.0–0.9s — COLD OPEN, NO TITLE CARD
Shot: already tight on the Park Lane square, filling most of frame. The 1935 figure is legible on it.
On-screen (bottom third, static): PARK LANE
Rank badge (top right of the square, static): 2nd dearest

0.9–3.0s — THE REVERSAL
Action: the 1935 figure snaps out and the real 2026 figure snaps in, hard cut, no dissolve. The badge flips.
Rank badge changes to: 6th cheapest
No other text. Hold dead still for a full second so the swap lands. Nothing else moves on screen.

3.0–6.0s — ORBIT ONE
Action: camera pushes back and orbits left across the board, continuous move, no cuts.
Badge flips on Bond Street as it passes: 20th of 22 → 1st
Caption under the badge, small, appears with it and stays 1.5s: median price paid; some commercial transfers included

6.0–8.5s — ORBIT TWO
Action: orbit continues.
Badge flips on Regent Street: 18th → 4th cheapest

8.5–11.0s — ORBIT THREE
Action: orbit slows and settles on Old Kent Road.
Badge appears and does NOT flip: still last
Caption below it, 1.5s: £60 in 1935. £325,000 in 2026.

11.0–13.0s — THE SPREAD
Shot: cut to a plain caption card over a slow, near-static wide of the board, heavily darkened so the text dominates.
On-screen, two lines, second line appears 0.4s after the first:
the old ladder spanned 6.7x
this one spans 103x

13.0–17.0s — PROVENANCE (REAL CAPTURE, NOT ANIMATION)
Shot: cut back to the live board. A finger or cursor taps a square. The provenance chip opens.
Visible in frame and held legible for a minimum of 2.5s: the HM Land Registry transaction ID, the transaction date, and the licence line.
On-screen caption, top of frame, static through the whole beat: every price. every square.
No motion during this beat beyond the chip opening — the viewer needs to read the ID.

17.0–21.0s — THE GATE FIRES
Shot: hard cut. A fabricated figure is planted into the build (show the value being written in for half a second, no code walls, just the number appearing where it should not be). Cut straight to the game being started.
The game refuses to load. The refusal screen appears with its reason line printed.
On-screen caption, appearing 0.5s after the refusal screen, bottom third: it will not start with a number it cannot source
This is the only engineering shot in the film. No zooms, no shake, no flourish.

21.0–24.0s — HOLD
Shot: the refusal screen, dead still, fully legible, reason line readable at phone size.
Single line of text beneath it, nothing else: [URL]
Freeze the final frame for a full second so the still thumbnail and any paused scroll show the machine saying no, not a pretty board.

NOTES FOR EDIT
- No call to action on screen at any point. That lives in the post copy.
- No face, no title card, no intro, no outro, no branding.
- No captions overlap: only one text element on screen at a time except where stated.
- Every figure shown must be one of the real board figures. Do not add any number to the film that is not on the board.
- If the Bond Street badge is on screen, the commercial-transfer caption must be on screen with it. Never one without the other.
- Cut on movement, not on beats — there is no music to cut to.
drafts.firstComment:
Sources and method, for anyone who wants to check the numbers rather than take my word for them.

Play it here: [URL]

PRICE DATA
All 2026 prices from HM Land Registry open data — Price Paid Data and the UK House Price Index. Contains HM Land Registry data © Crown copyright and database right 2026. This data is licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0. No subscription data sources were used anywhere in the build.

Method: median price paid per street, with the HM Land Registry transaction ID and URI carried on each square. 21 of the 22 streets resolve to actual recorded transactions. Trafalgar Square has no residential sale on record, so it falls back to the UK HPI borough average — stated on the square itself.

Known weakness, disclosed on each affected square: the median price paid method mixes some commercial transfers into a few streets. Bond Street's £33,575,353 is the figure most affected by this. Treat it as recorded evidence with that caveat attached, not as a residential value.

THE INTEGRITY GATE
141 monetary values, roughly 1,700 text nodes and 99 strings baked into WebGL textures, swept on every load. Any value without a provenance chain back to the facts file halts the build and prints the reason. Absence check, not spot check.

Verified by attack rather than assertion — 8 adversarial injections: an unsourced value tagged as traced, an untagged value, a banned term, trade dress, a fabricated figure baked into a 3D texture, an undeclared numeral, and two fabricated rounded values whose entire rounding band contains no real figure. All 8 caught.

EVENT CARDS
21 kept, each with source and date, drawn from gov.uk, the Bank of England and the ONS. 14 rejected as unverifiable. A second adversarial fact-check then corrected 7 more cards whose wording overstated its own source.

The rejection worth flagging: the widely repeated "commercial EPC C by 2027, B by 2030". The 2027 and 2030 commercial EPC targets remain consultation, not enacted law. I'll post the full sourcing on that separately.

VISUAL COMPARISON
Screenshots compared against real screenshots of Catan Universe, labels stripped, matched dimensions, three independent judges per comparison, each with a different lens, positions swapped and run twice. Desktop 2-1, both runs. Mobile 3-0, both runs.

OUTSTANDING
The data panel has not passed its own Financial Times standards review — 71 out of 82 at the last check. That is a fail and it is still open.

PROVENANCE
Original homage to Elizabeth Magie's The Landlord's Game, 1904, US Patent 748,626, public domain. Win condition is rent roll, per her original design. None of the trade dress, colours, square names or typography of any later commercial game.
drafts.altText: A 3D board game rendered in a web browser, viewed from above at an angle, showing a square board of 22 property spaces named after classic London streets. Each space displays a 2026 price in pounds taken from HM Land Registry data, alongside a small rank badge comparing its position on the 1935 printed board with its position today. The Park Lane space is highlighted in the foreground, its badge reading "2nd dearest in 1935, 6th cheapest in 2026". A provenance panel is open beside it showing an HM Land Registry transaction identifier, the transaction date, and an Open Government Licence v3.0 attribution line.

verdict.whyWinner:
It wins on the criterion that matters most, and it wins on a detail the other two fail at.

CREDIBILITY. craftLed is the only draft that lists all eight adversarial injections. dataLed announces "Eight adversarial injections:" and then lists seven — unsourced-but-tagged, untagged, banned term, texture-baked figure, undeclared numeral, two rounded values. Trade dress is missing. storyLed does exactly the same: says eight, lists seven. A post whose entire thesis is "I do not let unverified numbers reach the screen" cannot miscount its own list of eight. Someone will count. In UK CRE, someone always counts, and that comment becomes the post. craftLed lists all eight, on separate lines, and is internally consistent throughout. That single difference is worth more than everything else on this page.

STRUCTURE. craftLed is the only one that puts the discipline first and treats the game as the venue rather than the achievement — which is what the agreed angle actually argues for. dataLed executes the agreed running order (reversal, then rule) but its pivot line, "But the prices aren't the point", is the weakest sentence in any of the three: it tells the reader the last 180 words were a warm-up. craftLed's equivalent move — "The thing it happens to be attached to is a playable 3D board game... which I will come to" — earns the same pivot without discarding what came before.

METHOD. craftLed is the only draft carrying the blind comparison, and it handles it correctly: labels stripped, matched dimensions, three judges, positions swapped, run twice, then "Draw your own conclusion from that; it is a method, not a scalp." That paragraph is the single most institutional thing in the whole set. Dropping it, as the other two do, throws away the one piece of evidence that pre-empts "yes, but does it look like a school project".

storyLed loses outright. It opens with a history lecture — "In 1904 a woman patented a board game" — and the London price reversal, the actual scroll-stop for this audience, does not arrive until the eighth line, far below the fold. It also contains a plain factual error ("eighty years of London"; 1935 to 2026 is ninety-one) and an editorial nudge toward the Georgist thesis ("because it is the only honest one") that the brief explicitly told you to stay off.

REACH — applies to all three, and it is disqualifying as written. By my count each post runs 630 to 660 words, roughly 3,400 to 3,700 characters. LinkedIn's hard post limit is 3,000. None of these will post. Cut 15 to 20 per cent before you touch anything else; in craftLed the cuttable fat is the second half of the injection list (compress the two rounded values into one clause), "It does not sample. It asks the whole surface." (redundant with the sentence above it), and the Magie provenance block, which can lose ten words. The first comment is worse: at roughly 380 words it is around 2,200 characters against a 1,250-character comment limit. It needs to be two comments, and the second one will be seen by almost nobody, so put price data, the gate and the outstanding failure in comment one and push the visual comparison and provenance to comment two.

Other reach notes: no hashtags in any draft — correct, leave it. Link in body plus link in first comment is duplication; pick the body, because the whole CTA is "go and break it". The bounty line — "Find a number on that board that has no source behind it... I will publish the fix and credit you" — is the best comment-generating device here and it is identical in all three; keep it, and expect the first replies to be about Bond Street.

Timing: today is Monday 10 August 2026. The next slot that fits the brief is Tuesday 11 August, morning. That is one day, and the URL is not live. Do not post to hit the day.

FILLER CHECK. None of the three is generic AI slop — the numbers are too load-bearing and the disclosure is too specific. But each has a tell, and they are all the same tell: stage directions to the reader. dataLed: "That is the whole post, really." and "But the prices aren't the point." storyLed: "That is the fun part. Here is the actual experiment." craftLed: "The rule first, because the rule is the point." and "Now the venue, and the choice was deliberate." Cut all of these. A confident writer changes subject without announcing it. craftLed also has one smug construction — "in my own words rather than yours" — which reads as pre-emptive defensiveness; "Where it falls short:" is stronger and shorter. The closing three-block stack (live at URL / sources in first comment / message me) is verbatim identical across all three drafts, which is the clearest evidence these came off a template.
verdict.rewrittenOpening:
Park Lane is now the sixth cheapest street on the board. In 1935 it was the second dearest.

I trust that figure because the thing it sits on refuses to start if it finds a number it cannot source.

Not a warning. It stops, names the number, and prints why.

[Why this beats craftLed's original: the original opens on "I built something", which reads as a developer post and costs you the property professionals who scroll on engineering. This version buys the stop with two London streets and a reversal that completes in 91 characters — well inside the roughly 200-character fold on a phone — then spends that attention on the rule in line two, so the pivot happens above the fold rather than three paragraphs down. It keeps craftLed's best sentence intact. It also does the agreed angle's job properly: the reversal is the scroll-stop, the refusal is the argument, and line two welds them together instead of treating them as two separate posts stapled end to end.]
verdict.biggestWeakness:
The post's closing move is "It is live at [URL]. Find a number on that board that has no source behind it" — and per the brief it is not deployed. That is not a placeholder problem, it is a structural one. Everything craftLed does well is built on the transfer from "trust my claim" to "go and test my claim"; the bounty is what converts a boast into an experiment, and it is the only line in the post a sceptical MD can act on. Remove it and what remains is 600 words of unverifiable self-report about a private build — which is precisely the behaviour the post spends its whole length condemning. Ship it with a dead or coming-soon link and the first comment will be someone saying the link does not work, on a post about numbers that cannot be checked. There is no clever wording around this. Deploy first, or do not post.

Second-order, and worth fixing in the same pass: "the data panel has not passed its own Financial Times standards review — 71 out of 82" will be read by a meaningful share of readers as the Financial Times having reviewed and scored your work. "Its own" is doing more hedging than it can carry in a scanned feed. Reword to something like "an internal review against FT-style statistical presentation standards — 71 out of 82, still a fail, still open". The disclosure instinct is right; the phrasing accidentally borrows a masthead, which is exactly the class of unearned credibility the post exists to attack.
honestyFlags: ALL THREE DRAFTS, THE FIRST COMMENT AND THE VIDEO: 'It is live at [URL].' / 'Play it here: [URL]'. The brief states plainly that it is not yet deployed to a public URL. Every single version of this content asserts a live product. This is the largest honesty failure in the set and it is repeated five times.
dataLed: 'Eight adversarial injections:' followed by seven items. Trade dress is missing from the list. Count them.
storyLed: 'Eight adversarial injections —' followed by seven items. Same omission, same problem, in a post arguing for numerical discipline.

dataLed: 'which half our industry repeats as settled law'. The brief says 'widely-repeated'. 'Half our industry' is an invented quantity in the one paragraph where you are correcting other people's invented facts. Cut to 'which is widely repeated as settled law'.
storyLed: 'what eighty years of London did to the ranking'. 1935 to 2026 is ninety-one years. A wrong number, in a post about not publishing wrong numbers.
craftLed: 'nobody in a hundred years has asked where the £200 came from'. Same error class — the printed board is ninety-one years old, not a hundred.

ALL THREE: the '£200' pass-Go figure. Your own gate lists trade dress among the eight things it rejects, and then the copy borrows a specific monetary element of the commercial edition to make its joke. Either the rule applies to your prose or it does not. Rewrite as 'nobody has ever asked where the money on a board game came from'.

ALL THREE: the '£60' 1935 Old Kent Road price, and the whole 1935 ladder, are the commercial edition's printed prices. The post simultaneously claims to use none of that game's trade dress. This is defensible — printed prices are historical fact and you are citing, not reproducing — but be ready to say that sentence out loud, because it is the second thing a sharp commenter reaches for after Bond Street.

ALL THREE: 'the data panel has not passed its own Financial Times standards review — 71 out of 82'. Ambiguous to the point of misleading in a scanned feed; reads as the FT having assessed your work. Reword to name it as an internal review against FT presentation standards.

firstComment: 'Bond Street's £33,575,353 is the figure most affected by this.' The brief does not establish that Bond Street is the street most affected by commercial-transfer contamination — only that the method mixes commercial transfers into a few streets. You have invented a ranking inside your own methodology disclosure. Say 'Bond Street is among the streets affected' unless you can evidence the superlative.

storyLed: 'I've kept that scoring rule, because it is the only honest one'. That is an endorsement of the Georgist argument, which the brief told you to stay off. It is one clause and it will be the clause someone quotes.

craftLed: 'a fabricated figure baked into a WebGL texture where no text search would reach it'. Plausible, but it is a technical claim the brief does not make. Either you can demonstrate that a text search misses it or you cut the clause.

VIDEO: 'every price. every square.' shown over an HM Land Registry transaction ID. Twenty-one of twenty-two squares have a transaction ID. Trafalgar Square does not. This caption is the one statement in the entire package that your own gate would reject.

CREDIT WHERE DUE: all three drafts attach the commercial-transfer caveat to £33,575,353 in the same sentence, every time, without exception. All three label £33.6m as '(rounded)'. All three disclose the FT score, the median-method weakness and the Trafalgar Square fallback in the body rather than the comments. None names a model, mentions cost, or writes 'AI built'. The provenance line appears exactly once per draft. On the disclosure discipline the brief cared most about, the drafts are compliant.
americanisms: No American spellings found. Not one, across all three drafts, the first comment, the alt text and the video script. 'Analyse', 'organise', 'centre' traps were all avoided or not triggered; no '-ize' forms present.
Correct and non-trivial: 'licence attribution' (noun) alongside 'licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0' (verb). This is the exact pair most writers get wrong. It is right in every instance.

Not an Americanism but a house-style wobble: double quotation marks around "commercial EPC C by 2027, B by 2030". UK institutional style is single quotes. Cosmetic, but you are writing for readers who notice.

Not an Americanism but an inconsistency: dataLed opens with 'sixth cheapest' then uses '20th of 22', '2nd cheapest', '4th cheapest' within the same post. craftLed does the same, mixing 'sixth cheapest' with '20th of 22'. Pick words or pick numerals. In a post about presentation rigour, mixed ordinals are a small self-inflicted wound.
Not an Americanism but check before posting: '2-1' and '3-0' use hyphens; UK typesetting takes an en dash for score ranges. Trivial, and LinkedIn will not preserve it anyway. Ignore if you want.
verdict.videoAudit:
DOES IT WORK MUTED: yes, structurally. No voiceover, captions burned in, one text element on screen at a time, eight per cent safe margins, no reliance on music. The beats sum to exactly 24.0 seconds, which suggests someone actually added them up. That is the baseline and it clears it.

But two beats will not be readable in practice, and they are the two that matter most.

At 3.0 to 6.0 seconds the mandatory Bond Street caveat — 'median price paid; some commercial transfers included' — is specified as small type, appearing under a badge, during a continuous camera orbit, held for 1.5 seconds. That is the single most legally and reputationally load-bearing caption in the film and you have made it the least legible thing in it: small, moving, brief. On a phone in a feed it will not be read. Fix: stop the orbit dead for the Bond Street beat, set the caveat at the same size as the badge, and hold it for 2.5 seconds minimum. Your own edit note says the caption must never be on screen without the badge — good — but the note should be stronger: the badge must never be on screen without a legible caption.

At 13.0 to 17.0 seconds you ask for an HM Land Registry transaction ID to be held legible for 2.5 seconds in a 1:1 frame at phone size. HMLR transaction identifiers are long alphanumeric strings. At 1080 by 1080, viewed at phone scale, that will render as a grey smear that reads as 'some sort of reference number' rather than as evidence. That is actually fine as an impression — but then do not ask the viewer to read it. Either crop hard to a fragment of the ID plus the licence line at large type, or accept it as texture and put the weight on the caption.

IS THE FIRST FRAME ARRESTING: no, and there is a real mechanical error here. The cold open is a tight shot of Park Lane showing the 1935 figure and a '2nd dearest' badge. As a still — which is what a scrolling user sees for the first fraction of a second, and what LinkedIn uses as the default thumbnail — that is a board square with an old number on it. It shows the state you are about to disprove, not the disproof. Worse, the edit note says 'Freeze the final frame for a full second so the still thumbnail and any paused scroll show the machine saying no'. That assumes the thumbnail comes from the end of the video. It does not; LinkedIn takes an early frame unless you upload a custom one. So the note is describing an outcome the platform will not produce. Either upload the refusal screen as a custom thumbnail, or restructure so frame zero already carries the reversal — for example open on Park Lane with both badges present, '2nd dearest 1935' struck through and '6th cheapest 2026' beneath it, hold half a second, then run the swap animation for viewers who stay.
